stops.name: Djemaa Ghazaouet, the surrender
stops.campa: Beaten, his territory reduced to a shrinking strip of the Moroccan border, Abd al-Qadir crosses the Oued Kiss and offers General Lamoricière his surrender in exchange for safe passage to Alexandria or Acre — terms Lamoricière and the Duke of Aumale accept and put in writing. At the little port the French call Nemours he hands the duke his own warhorse, a soldier's gesture between soldiers, and passes his last night as a free ruler at Djemaa Ghazaouet. The promise of Alexandria or Acre will not be kept; the ship waiting for him sails instead for Toulon.

stops.name: Toulon, Fort Lamalgue
stops.campa: The ship lands its cargo of ninety-seven souls — the emir, his mother, his wives, his household — not at Alexandria but at Toulon, where they are marched into Fort Lamalgue and held four months while Paris decides, without consulting the men who signed the surrender terms, that the promise of exile in the East will not be honored. Louis-Philippe's government has captured a legend and does not intend to let him go anywhere he could raise a country again. The broken word will shadow every year of what follows.

stops.name: Pau, the château of the old kings
stops.campa: From Toulon the household is moved inland to the château of Pau, birthplace of Henri IV, for a further six months of a captivity that is honorable in form — rooms, not cells — and crushing in substance: a mountain people's household shut up through a foreign winter, uncertain if release will ever come, watching each other for the first signs of the sickness the damp French climate is already breeding among them.

stops.name: Amboise, four years, twenty-five graves
stops.campa: The household is settled at last in the château of Amboise on the Loire, and here it will remain nearly four years. The Loire valley's damp cold does what French guns could not: twenty-five of the emir's people, family and retainers both, sicken and die within these walls and are buried nearby, far from Algeria. Abd al-Qadir spends the years in study and prayer, refusing the bitterness his visitors expect of him; the town, watching the white burnous pass, takes him for its own, and in Paris Victor Hugo and Émile de Girardin campaign in print for a captive half of literary France admires more than it fears.
stops.quote: I leave, and I leave my heart with you.
stops.quote_source: Abdelkader's farewell to the people of Amboise on his departure, December 1852

stops.name: Amboise, freed by the future emperor
stops.campa: Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, Prince-President and soon to crown himself emperor, comes to Amboise in person against the advice of his own ministers and tells the emir he is free. You have been the enemy of France, he says, but I do justice to your courage, your character, your resignation in misfortune; this is why I hold it an honour to end your captivity, having full confidence in your word. Abd al-Qadir swears never to trouble Algeria again, is granted a pension, and stands among the guests at the proclamation of the Second Empire before sailing east at last — not to Algeria, but to Ottoman soil.
stops.quote: You have been the enemy of France, but I nonetheless do justice to your courage, your character, your resignation in misfortune; this is why I hold it an honour to put an end to your captivity, having full confidence in your word.
stops.quote_source: Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte to Abdelkader, Château d'Amboise, 16 October 1852

stops.name: Bursa, the years of exile begin
stops.campa: The Sultan grants him residence at Bursa, in Ottoman Anatolia, and here he settles his household anew: a pension from France, a sabre sent by Napoleon III engraved to Emir Abd-el-Kader-ben-Mahhi-ed-Din, three Arabian horses sent back in thanks. He is honored and idle at once, a general with no army and no war, a scholar with time at last for the studies the fighting years never allowed. He writes; he prays; he waits, not for Algeria, which he has sworn to leave alone, but for the shape his life will take now that the war is over and he is only forty-four.

stops.name: Bursa, the earthquake
stops.campa: A violent earthquake devastates Bursa in the early months of 1855, and in its ruin the emir sees a providence: a decent excuse to ask his sultan and his French pension-holder for a warmer, more scholarly exile. He travels that year to the Paris Exposition, presents to the Société Asiatique an Arabic manuscript titled Rappel à l'intelligent, avis à l'indifférent — the work later republished as Lettre aux Français, arguing for the deep kinship of Christian and Islamic wisdom — and by year's end has secured permission to remove his household to Damascus.

stops.name: Damascus, settling in the Amara quarter
stops.campa: Two hundred family members and retainers arrive to join the some five hundred Algerian exiles already settled in Damascus since the fall of the Emirate, a community that will grow past fifteen hundred within Abd al-Qadir's lifetime. He takes a house in the Amara quarter within walking distance of the tomb he prayed at as a boy of eighteen, thirty years gone. Damascus receives the famous prisoner-general as a scholar and a saint's neighbor, not as a curiosity; within weeks he is asked to teach.

stops.name: The Umayyad Mosque, teaching and the Mawaqif
stops.campa: Invited to teach in the great Umayyad Mosque at the city's heart, Abd al-Qadir gathers around him a circle of students in the Akbarian theosophy of Ibn Arabi and begins dictating the work that will occupy the rest of his life: the Kitab al-Mawaqif, the Book of Halts, hundreds of spiritual stations recorded as they come to him, direct and unmediated, in the manner of his master five centuries gone. The soldier's years recede; the commentator's begin. He is not yet fifty and believes, as far as anyone can tell, that the war is entirely behind him.

stops.name: Damascus, the refugees from Mount Lebanon
stops.campa: Word reaches Damascus of a Druze massacre of Maronite Christians in the mountains of Lebanon; thousands of survivors stream into the city seeking the safety a provincial capital is supposed to offer. Rumor runs the other way too — that Damascus's own Muslim quarters mean to finish what the mountain began. Abd al-Qadir, informed and alarmed, goes personally to the French consul and then to the Ottoman governor, Ahmad Pasha, urging measures to keep the peace; the governor does little. Under cover of secrecy the consul arms the emir and a thousand of his Algerian exiles at French expense, in case the alarm proves true.

stops.name: The Christian quarter, nine days of rescue
stops.campa: On the ninth of July the alarm proves true: armed mobs break into the Christian quarter, burning houses and killing without distinction. Abd al-Qadir and his armed Algerians move through the streets in the smoke, pulling families from burning courtyards, cutting through the crowd to reach consulates and convents; he offers fifty piastres a head to anyone who brings him a living Christian rather than a dead one. His house fills past capacity within a day; the overflow he moves, under his own guard, into the citadel, wrung reluctantly from the governor. Consuls, Lazarist priests, Daughters of Charity, some four hundred children, owe him, by the lowest count, their lives; other counts run past ten thousand.
stops.quote: As long as one of my soldiers is still standing, you will not touch them. They are my guests.
stops.quote_source: The emir to the mob at his own door, Damascus, July 1860, cited in Kiser, Commander of the Faithful

stops.name: Damascus, the letter to Bishop Pavy and the honors of the world
stops.campa: Thanked by the Catholic bishop of Algiers, Louis Pavy, for what he did for the Christians of Damascus, the emir answers in the plain register of his own law rather than of gratitude accepted: that which we did, we did to be faithful, not to any foreign creed, but to Islam itself. In the months after, medals and swords and rifles arrive from every court in Europe and from Abraham Lincoln in Washington; France doubles his pension and names him Grand Cross of the Legion of Honour. He accepts them as a soldier accepts decorations — gravely, and as evidence for a case larger than his own reputation, that the faith he was raised in commanded exactly what he did.
stops.quote: That which we did for the Christians, we did to be faithful to Islamic Law, and out of respect for human rights. The law places greatest importance on compassion and mercy and all that preserves social cohesion.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Bishop Louis Antoine Pavy of Algiers, 1860, cited in Kiser, Commander of the Faithful
